In the world of functional components, there are a few classic designs that seem to take forever to outlive their usefulness. In April 1952, Boeing first flew the Stratofortress that would soon be best known by its service designation-the B-52. Now nearly six decades later, the bomber is still in service and flown by USAF pilots who are younger than the planes themselves, the last of which rolled off the assembly line in 1962.

In the world that revolves around GM, there is a similar-sounding disc brake system used from 1968 well into the '90s called the D52, which is the FMSI designation for its brake pad style. The caliper's large, single-piston, floating design qualifies it as perhaps the single most commonly used front brake caliper in GM history.

The D52  universal use also makes it a popular choice for early GM muscle car cultists as an inexpensive disc brake swap, since the parts can probably be found in Nigeria if necessary. But it is also this caliper's popularity that forces many car crafters to choose something a little different. That's why Wilwood designed the new aluminum D52 aluminum caliper. Intended as a simple bolt-on upgrade, the Wilwood caliper differs from the original design by packaging two, smaller, stainless steel pistons that generate the same overall piston area as the single piston. The advantage is that the pair of pistons offers a wider apply surface to the back of the pad (4.240 inches versus 2.850 inches), creating a more stable load on the pads. The new Wilwood caliper operates in a similar fashion as the original design by floating the caliper on two pins that pull the outside pad into the rotor with a near-similar load as the inboard pad. The load applied to both pads is improved with the superior rigidity of the forged (not cast) aluminum body. While all this should improve the overall feel and performance of this caliper conversion, it doesn't hurt that these calipers also look cool. We decided to try a set of red-powdercoated  D52 calipers on our 455-powered '64 Olds F-85 that had previously been treated to an Original Parts Group, factory-style, '70 Chevelle disc brake conversion. Check out how this all went down.

The B-52's nickname is the BUFF: Big-Ugly Fat Fellow. There's a more colorful variation for the last F, but hey, there are children present.

The installation on our street-driven Olds F-85 couldn't have been easier. A couple of years ago, we bolted on an OPG disc brake conversion kit to which we had converted to a set of Performance Friction pads that definitely improved pedal feel and stopping distance as well. Bolting on these new Wilwood calipers is pretty simple.

Tech tip: Never return the utensils to the kitchen after you use them in the shop. Deny everything.

Few magazine stories on installing high-performance brake systems ever mention that new pads must be bedded properly beforehand to achieve maximum performance. Even normal driving may not achieve sufficient temperature to properly bed the pads. The procedure accomplishes this final heat cycle for the brake material. This is important for race cars, but track time is expensive, so Wilwood offers a service that will bed a set of pads. For street cars, however, this isn't necessary, as Wilwood publishes a very specific bedding process that we've included in the accompanying chart. What you do not want to do is bolt on a new set of pads and then immediately abuse the brakes in a competition situation such as a road course track day. Excessive heat applied too quickly can cause the pad material to crack or glaze, neither of which will produce optimal pad performance. This bedding process also allows the pads to transfer a small amount of material onto the rotor surface, which optimizes the coefficient of friction to the rotor. Allow 20 to 30 seconds between each step to stabilize the brake temperature.

As cars, trucks, and SUVs become increasingly electrified, their hardware will also slowly head towards a more digital era. Braking systems, up until recently, have all mostly relied on an antiquated, yet highly redundant technique of using hydraulics to squeeze a caliper onto a rotating disc called the rotor. But when electric vehicles (EVs) came to be, their ability to slow the car down using the electric motor's change of direction, through regenerative braking, gave us a new look at how modern vehicles can come to a stop.

Automotive parts suppliers Brembo and ZF's latest developments in braking technology don't rely on regenerative braking to revolutionize the way brakes operate. But their brake-by-wire technology takes inspiration from EVs, and could soon signal the end of the traditional hydraulic braking system.

A New, "Dry" Type Of Brake-By-Wire System

Close up on wheel assembly with rotor and Brembo caliper Toyota

Detail shot of the 19-inch wheels and standard Brembo brakes as seen on a blue 2024 Genesis G70 3.3T AWD Sport Photo: Justin Kaehler

Close up on wheel assembly with rotor and Brembo caliper Toyota

Detail shot of the 19-inch wheels and standard Brembo brakes as seen on a blue 2024 Genesis G70 3.3T AWD Sport Photo: Justin Kaehler

Brake-by-wire technology isn't new. Introduced about a decade ago, the idea behind it is to reduce the amount of mechanical components required to complete a car's full braking system. Essentially, what these first systems did was send a signal from your brake pedal to an electronic master cylinder, which then still relied on the system's hydraulic pressure to move the caliper around.

But, what both Brembo and ZF are working on moves the needle a tad further. Brembo will be the first to put its Sensify system onto the market as early as this year, while ZF's Electro-Mechanical Braking (EMB) system is scheduled for 2028.

What these "dry" systems effectively do is delete the entire brake booster and brake lines, essentially getting rid of the entire hydraulic system in the process. ZF's approach is very much like that of a racing simulator. The brake pedal sends a signal to a small electric motor installed within the brake caliper itself, telling it to squeeze the caliper according to pedal force. But this system suggests only using electric motors on the rear brakes. The front brakes would still rely on the traditional hydraulic system, for reliability reasons, ZF says. From Diego Cusi, ZF's director of engineering:

A pedal simulator observes driver intent though pedal travel and force and translates it into a signal that is processed through a central computer. That signal is now going to be issued out to the four corners.

What's also interesting about this system is that the current feeling of the anti-lock brake system (ABS) kicking in will disappear. This is caused by the fact that the brake-by-wire system is never actually connected to the brake pedal itself. Some will say that such a system will completely delete the brake pedal feel, and these people would be right. But carmakers have already surprised us in the realm of electronic power steering systems. So I'm not too worried.

Brembo Wants To Favor A Fully Electric System

Close up shot of the wheels on a purple 2024 BMW Z4, featuring the M Sport Brakes BMW

The brakes of a 2024 Mercedes-AMG E53 Hybrid 4Matic+ Mercedes-Benz

A close up shot of the wheels and brakes on a 2023 Dodge Challenger Black Ghost Mecum

The glowing brakes of the 2025 Aston Martin Vantage Aston Martin

Close up shot of the wheels on a purple 2024 BMW Z4, featuring the M Sport Brakes BMW

The brakes of a 2024 Mercedes-AMG E53 Hybrid 4Matic+ Mercedes-Benz

A close up shot of the wheels and brakes on a 2023 Dodge Challenger Black Ghost Mecum

The glowing brakes of the 2025 Aston Martin Vantage Aston Martin

Brembo's system, however, is much more advanced, and could be of great use in the EV space. While ZF suggests a "hybrid" brake-by-wire system, Brembo would prefer moving forward with electric motors on all four wheels. However, only an EV could supply an electrical system powerful enough to sustain such a system. Hence why ZF believes its integration of both electronics and hydraulics would work better with gasoline-powered vehicles equipped with 48-volt mild hybrid systems.

In both cases, however, these technologies elevate braking systems to a whole new level, with many benefits, such as cost-reduction and reduced weight from the absence of brake lines and boosters. While the caliper itself is heavier due to the integrated electric motors, brake-by-wire remains overall lighter and less expensive to manufacture, to say nothing of the reduced maintenance costs down the line.

That's because these systems don’t require brake fluid flushes. Brake pads will also last longer, and fuel economy is expected to improve, since electronic brake calipers do without the traditional drag effect caused by conventional systems. Neither Brembo nor ZF have said in which vehicles their systems will be integrated first, but my guess is that high-end, luxury vehicles will be first on the list.

Copper Under Pressure: What the Shift to Copper-Free Brake Pads Means for Fleets

With copper-free brake standards taking effect, suppliers are reengineering friction materials, and fleets are weighing what the change means for air disc brake performance on the road. Find out more in this Heavy Duty Trucking Digital Cover Story for March 2026.

Copper has been used in brake friction materials for more than a century. What happens when it's no longer an option? What trucking fleets need to know.

A national transition to copper-free brake pads has affected friction material formulations.

These changes in brake materials have a greater impact on air disc brakes.

Some trucking fleets are frustrated by increased maintenance costs for ADBs.

The shift has been a significant challenge for suppliers to innovate while maintaining brake efficiency and reliability.

For decades, copper has quietly done some of the hardest work in heavy-duty truck braking systems.

It stabilized friction. It pulled heat out of the pad. It reinforced the friction matrix. It helped create the all-important transfer film that makes air disc brakes perform smoothly under punishing duty cycles.

And now, it’s effectively gone.

Are Brake Pads Wearing out Faster Without Copper? OEM brake suppliers say N-level copper-free pads meet durability and FMVSS-121 stopping standards. However, some fleets report higher wear in certain duty cycles, particularly when friction specifications don’t match the application. Proper spec’ing and maintenance appear to be key variables.

As of Jan. 1, 2025, brake pads sold in and Washington must contain less than 0.5% copper by weight. This is a threshold widely considered “copper-free” by regulatory agencies.

While the laws originated at the state level, the industry has standardized nationally around compliant friction formulations rather than building state-specific pads.

For fleets, the transition has been largely invisible. However, some fleet managers are raising concerns that reduced-copper or copper-free air disc brake linings aren’t holding up as well in certain operations.

A few have even floated the idea of stepping back from air disc brakes altogether, especially on trailers. That’s a serious claim in a market where air disc brake (ADB) adoption in linehaul applications now exceeds 50%.

So, what’s really going on?

To understand the impact, it helps to start at the beginning and understand why copper became so central to heavy truck braking in the first place.

Why Copper Was Critical in Heavy-Duty Brake Pads

Copper has been used in brake friction materials for more than a century. According to Richard Conklin, Director of Engineering, Wheel End, Bendix Commercial Vehicle Systems, its use dates back to 1913. It became widespread by 1918, often in mesh or screen form to reinforce friction materials.

Over time, copper became a staple in both disc pad and drum lining formulations for commercial vehicles.

The Case for Air Disc Brakes

“Copper has been used as an additive in brake friction formulations for decades,” says J eff Morris , director, axle, brake, and wheel-end systems, Hendrickson. “It was widely adopted in the 1980s as the industry evolved away from older formulations that included lead.”

Its appeal wasn’t based on a single magic property. Rather, it was an important component in a combination of friction materials.

Julia Cilleruelo Fernandez del Moral, senior product marketing specialist for Cummins Drivetrain and Braking Systems (formerly Meritor ), compares brake pad formulation to baking cookies.

“Pad formulas contain four main functional groups,” she explains. “These include fibers, fillers, friction modifiers, and resins. And each contains up to 20 different elements or compounds.

"Engineers often describe it like a cookie recipe. That’s because if you swap out a single ingredient, it can change the texture, structure, or how the brake pad behaves.”

And while copper wasn’t the only ingredient in the brake pad recipe, it was most certainly an important one.

Why Air Disc Brakes Relied Heavily on Copper

It was arguably even more important for air disc brakes. Because they generally operate at higher temperatures than drums, many air disc brake pads are semi-metallic and contained more copper.

Sudhive Nair, head of chassis control North America at ZF, explains that copper served multiple roles in air disc brake pads:

It acted as a friction modifier, helping stabilize the coefficient of friction.

It reinforced the pad structure alongside steel fibers.

It conducted heat efficiently away from the friction surface.

It helped form and stabilize the transfer layer — the thin film that disc brakes rely on for consistent, predictable stopping.

In disc brakes especially, Nair explains, copper’s ability to smear and fill surface asperities helped promote an even transfer film between pad and rotor. That stability is critical during heavy braking events.

Surface asperities are the microscopic peaks and valleys on a brake pad and rotor surface — the tiny high spots where contact and heat begin during braking. Copper helps fill in those irregularities and promotes a smoother, more stable friction layer between pad and rotor.

Why Copper Is Being Phased Out

So why is copper suddenly on the outs? The issue isn’t performance. It’s environmental impact.

Copper particles from brake wear can wash into stormwater systems and eventually reach waterways. Research has shown that elevated copper levels can be toxic to aquatic life, especially salmon.

In 2010, California and Washington passed laws (often referred to as the Better Brakes Law) to limit copper and other heavy metals in brake friction materials.

From an OEM perspective, there was understandably little appetite for producing different pad formulations for different states. Instead, the industry standardized around compliant friction.

In 2015, industry groups partnered with the Environmental Protection Agency under a Memorandum of Understanding to voluntarily phase down copper content.

To comply with new regulations, pads are now clearly labeled by compliance level:

B-Level (≤5% copper) by 2021

N-Level (≤0.5% copper) by 2025

Enforcement focuses on manufacture and sale, not end users. That means existing parts inventory can still be used, and that fleets are not at risk of being cited for running older pads.

Some trucking fleets don't feel that the new reduced-copper formulations are living up to the same standard.

Replacing Copper: No Silver Bullet

Removing copper wasn’t as simple as swapping one ingredient for another.

“There is no single 1:1 replacement,” Nair says. “Formulations shift by increasing steel fiber reinforcement and using more complex combinations of lubricants, abrasives, and modifiers.”

Silicon, steel, iron, and proprietary metallurgy and resin compounds can serve as functional substitutes, adds Conklin at Bendix Commercial Vehicle Systems.

“Brake friction remains an innovative space," he says. "Silicon, steel, iron and other proprietary metallurgy and resin compounds can act as functional substitutes for copper. Every application is different, and every route demands something different from the truck. But our expectation is similar performance between the outgoing materials and the new N-level pads.”

Regardless of the materials selected, Hendrickson emphasizes that brakes must be engineered as a system.

“In a disc brake, the pad and rotor are developed as a friction couple,” Morris explains. “Using non-OE replacement pads can affect rotor life, even if the pad itself appears to perform well.”

In some applications, Hendrickson required adjustments to brake chamber sizes to maintain torque output with N-level friction.

[IMG:1]

According to Cilleruelo Fernandez del Moral, Cummins spent four to five years developing and validating N-level formulas through laboratory testing, FMVSS validation, and fleet trials.

As a result, its current N-level friction used in Meritor EX+ LS, EX+ L, EX+ H and Quadraulic disc brakes meets or exceeds previous wear and performance expectations, she says.

Nair says ZF put more than 10 million test miles on reduced-copper pads to determine their capabilities. The company also conducted additional million-mile tests on zero-copper pads. And both pad types met all required durability standards.

From an OEM standpoint, the message is consistent: Performance parity has been achieved.

Why Are Some Fleets Concerned?

Brent Hickman, senior manager of equipment and maintenance at Pilot Company, says he’s seen the company’s total maintenance costs increase by about 21% year over year, and a big part of that is brakes. Pilot specs air disc brakes on both tractor and trailer.

The company brake wear has decreased between 28% and 35% depending on whether it's the truck or trailer. The cost of brakes and brake repair have risen about 26% year over year.

Hickman says the materials that met the B-level standard starting in 2021 are now at the point where “less than desired” brake pad wear has become evident.

"We're at that point in the life cycle of the fleet that have these new pads where we're seeing a ton of failures," he says. And those failures also cause damage to rotors and calipers.

He believes part of the problem is that some of the materials used to replace copper produce a vapor or fog that creates a sticky coating on pads and rotors and degrades performance.

"I'm at the point now, I'm almost ready to go back to drum brakes on the trailers. And I know four fleets have done that. Problem is … it's not an immediate gain. I'm not going to go swap all the trailers over that are currently discs to drums. That's about 12 grand a trailer."

Tips for Copper-Free Brake Adoption by Fleets

Suppliers have some advice for fleets to help avoid problems.

Air disc brake adoption has surged over the past several years, particularly in linehaul applications. But, of course, not all duty cycles are created equal.

“Some applications are better suited for air disc brakes than others,” explains Cilleruelo Fernandez del Moral. “Duty cycle and operating environment can influence pad life.”

One potential issue is misapplication.

“If a fleet selects a linehaul N-type friction mix and uses it in a severe-service application, they may experience higher wear,” she says. “That would be the same if they used an A-type linehaul pad in a severe-service application.”

In other words, copper-free friction isn’t inherently weaker — but it still must match the job.

Maintenance practices also matter.

Disc brake pad wear inspection requires wheel removal, which some fleets defer. If pads wear beyond recommended limits, progressive rotor damage can occur. This can dramatically increase repair costs.

To address this, Cummins is working with OEMs to deploy electronic pad wear indicators and explore predictive sensing technologies.

"Of course there are offsets to performance when substituting these other materials for copper that affect overall torque output and wear performance at various temperatures," says Keith McComsey, technical sales lead (wheel-end) at Bendix Commercial Vehicle Systems. "So it is a delicate balance to try to maintain those levels of performance with these other materials."

McComsey says fleets concerned about performance issues should ask OEMs and brake manufacturers if there are differences in torque output and wear so they are educated as to the safety impacts from previous lining materials to the new materials being used today.

"Keeping in mind, though," he adds, "that brake manufacturers and OEMs are mandated to still maintain FMVSS-121 standards for reduced stopping distances and parking capabilities."

EPA copper-free brake initiative moves to next phase

With the first phase of the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Copper-Free Brake Initiative coming to a close at the end of the year, Bendix Commercial Vehicle Systems reminds fleets and owner-operators to make sure they’re keeping up with the necessary changes in aftermarket air disc brake (ADB) friction formulation.

“It’s important that fleets, distributors, and everyone who does brake pad changes is aware of what’s going on with various Bendix replacement pads and labeling,” said Keith McComsey, Bendix director of Air Disc Brake and Systems. “And with the significant increase in ADB adoption over the past decade, there’s a particular interest in ADB pad changes.”

In January 2015, organizations within the automotive and commercial vehicle industries – including trucking – signed onto the Copper-Free Brake Initiative, along with the EPA and the Environmental Council of the States. This action was taken because copper from stormwater runoff can be harmful to the environment, affecting plants and animals – and when used in brake pads, it makes its way into the air and water through the fine dust released from friction during braking.

In 2010, according to EPA estimates, vehicular braking in California alone released 1.3 million pounds of copper into the environment. That year, both California and Washington passed laws reducing the amount of copper permitted in brake pads.

B-Level compliance, or phase 2, of the initiative takes effect on Jan. 1, 2021, and limits the amount of copper to no more than 5% by weight. Other material limits remain unchanged. In January 2025, copper’s limit will drop to 0.5% – one-half of 1% – by weight for N-Level compliance. The agreement also commits participants to take steps to educate the automotive and trucking industries on the changes and provides guidelines for marking and labeling friction material packaging and products.

[IMG:1]

“Even though many Bendix friction materials have been compliant with the 2021 standards for a long time, some older aftermarket ADB pads will be phasing out of compliance at the end of the year,” McComsey said. “For customers currently using these, we’ve been including postcards with the replacement kits letting them know about the change and pointing them to the compliant friction.”

The A-Level-compliant frictions, which include both the Bendix BX275 OE-level friction and the aftermarket BA235, will become obsolete. The suitable B-Level copper-compliant replacements are the Bendix BX276 and BX283 pads, which are OE-level pads already available in the North American market. Both will remain compliant through 2024, while providing longer friction life and meeting FMVSS-121 stopping distance and park hold requirements. Bendix will also launch the BA236 pad in 2021, an aftermarket friction that will be B-Level copper-compliant through 2024.

Bendix parts and replacement kit numbers involved are:

BX275 – obsolete Dec. 31, 2020

BA235 – obsolete Dec. 31, 2020

BX276 – available; compliant through 2024

BX283 – available; compliant through 2024

BA236 – coming in 2021; compliant through 2024

Bendix wheel-end solutions include air disc and drum brake systems, automatic slack adjusters, spring brakes, friction, and remanufactured brake shoes that provide lower total cost of ownership while delivering on safety, stopping power, and reliability. Bendix helps fleets and drivers in the areas most critical to their success by improving vehicle performance and efficiency, and by backing its products with unparalleled post-sales support. By strengthening return on investment in the technologies that improve vehicle and driver safety, Bendix supports safer North American roads for all who share them.

“When Phase 3 of the initiative rolls around on Jan. 1, 2025, Bendix will be ready for that too,” McComsey said. “We’re already engineering copper-compliant ADB friction for the most stringent level, with plans for production to begin well in advance of the deadline.”

SEATTLE – Manufacturers of brake pads are gearing up to meet a first-in-the-nation Washington state law requiring they phase out the use of copper and other heavy metals.

Washington in 2010 banned the use of copper in brake pads, as a way to prevent the metal from polluting waters and harming fish. When brakes wear down, they release copper shavings onto roads that are eventually washed into rivers, where, state officials say, they could harm marine life, especially salmon.

“We’re hoping that people will be ready to certify their products soon,” said Ian Wesley, the law’s coordinator. He added: “I’m expecting that people will want to certify quickly.”

The first phase of the law takes effect Jan. 1, when manufacturers of friction brakes will be required to report the concentrations of heavy metals such as copper, zinc or nickel in their products.

Brake pads manufactured after 2015 may not contain asbestos, mercury, cadmium or other heavy metals. By 2021, brake pads must contain less than five percent copper. The allowable amount of copper could drop almost to zero in 2023 if manufacturers show it is possible.

California passed a similar law in September 2010. California’s law requires brake pad manufacturers to reduce copper in brake pads sold in that state to no more than 5 percent by 2021, and no more than 0.5 percent by 2025.

The laws in Washington and California will likely mean that copper-free pads will become the industry standard in the U.S.

“Once California passed their law, it became obvious that that will be the national standard,” said Ann Wilson, senior vice president of government affairs with Motor & Equipment Manufacturers Association, which represents manufacturers of motor vehicle parts and systems for use in light- and heavy-duty vehicles.

Industry officials say it is possible some manufacturers will begin to market brake pads with lower amounts of copper ahead of those deadlines.

“You’ll see a number of manufacturers try to get the appropriate product out there as soon as they possibly can. Some may make it before the deadline,” Wilson said. “I think consumers are going to start seeing product out there in fairly short order.”

In Washington, brake manufacturers must use accredited laboratories and self-certify to the state that their brake pads comply with the law. All brake pads manufactured after Jan. 1, 2015, must be marked on both the pad and its packaging.

Both states have agreed on a common marking system that will be used to identify compliant products, according to the state.

Many brake pads are made of steel, brass and copper fibers – materials designed to create friction and draw off heat. Some contain ceramics, Kevlar and other nonmetallic compounds. Some already contain zero or low amounts of copper.

In 2011, the state also banned copper-based bottom paint on recreational boats, or those 65 feet and under. New recreational boats with copper-based bottom paint may not be sold in Washington state after Jan. 1, 2018, and the sale of paint with more than 0.5 percent copper is prohibited on boats as of 2020.

Disc brake pads are to brakes what a camshaft is to an engine. Where a cam is critical for defining an engine's power potential, brake pads are vital for successfully and repeatedly decelerating a vehicle. Experienced hot rodders know there are a ton of variables when it comes to cam selection, with no one grind being the best for every situation. Likewise, brake engineers must juggle system wear characteristics, operating temperature range, harshness, dust, noise, environmental factors, material and manufacturing costs, and even individual driver preferences. For the serious racer, brake pad choice is a continually evolving process, changing on a nearly monthly basis.

The higher a brake pad's coefficient of friction (expressed by the Greek letter , pronounced mu), the more aggressive the pad and the greater its stopping potential (the same amount of pedal force provides more stopping power). In theory,  ranges from 0 (full lubricity, no friction at all) to 1.0 (solid, no molecules moving). Fifteen to 20 years ago, Baer brakes says, street brake pads were lucky to see the high 0.20s. Today, even OEM pads are well into the 0.30s, top-tier performance street pads in the 0.40 to 0.45 range, and some race cars in the high 0.60s.

A pad's friction is not constant, varying due to changes in temperature, humidity, wear, age, and many other factors. Pad designers strive to develop more stable pad compounds that maintain consistency over a wide range of operating conditions. But as compounds become more exotic, they also become more expensive. And more aggressive (higher ) compounds may increase rotor wear. There's no free lunch.

The friction performance of pads intended for typical street temperatures is classified under SAE Standard J866, expressed as a two-letter code where the first letter designates the low-temperature (0 to 200 degrees F) friction performance and the second letter the high-temperature (200 to 600 degrees F) performance. The letters generally appear on the backing plate as a prefix or suffix to the part number. If the first letter is lower than the second, the pad works better at high temperatures and needs a warm-up; if the second letter is lower than the first, the pad may fade at high temperatures. The best street pads have good friction at both high and low temperatures (ideally, both letters would be the same, as in FF).

Not all pads are marked this way. Full-race pads may operate at high temperature ranges outside of the classification range. And some manufacturers use proprietary classifications, such as color-coding the pads or their own numbering schemes.

Is it time to get your
brake pads changed
? Before you choose just any set of brake pads, it'd be best to get familiar with all the different brake types available. You could save some money or improve your performance with a simple change. There are four types of brake pads available on the market: Organic, ceramic, metallic, and semi-metallic. Sometimes, manufacturers will call some of these pad types something else, such as non-asbestos organic or NAO brake pads.

Naming schemes aside, when you're looking at brake pads, you're looking at pads made of one of the material types listed above. Take a look at the list of materials on a manufacturer's page for the brake pads you're looking at, and you can quickly determine which type of brake pad you're looking at. Generally, fully metallic brakes are not common in the consumer market, so you'll be looking at brake pads made of organic materials, a combination of metals and other materials, or are made from ceramic.

They all have specific advantages and disadvantages in areas like durability, noise, cost, and the amount of dust they create. No brake pad material will be perfect for everyone, but with the proper knowledge, you'll be able to identify the type that's best for your needs.

[IMG:1]

Organic brake pads have an interesting history. Originally, these brake pads (among other car components) had asbestos in them, and it was a commonly used material. Some overseas brands still use it today, though the material is slowly being phased out. If you replace your own brake pads and have an older vehicle, make sure you're properly protecting yourself against asbestos dust.

Today, organic brake pads, or Non-Asbestos Organic (NAO) brake pads, are more commonly used in the U.S. Organic brake pads use a mix of materials such as fiberglass, rubber, and sometimes Kevlar bonded with a resin. This creates brake pads that are softer than the other options on the market, which makes for a quieter stop. Organic brake pads are also some of the cheaper options on the market.

While these are all benefits, organic brake pads have some drawbacks. These types of pads will wear down quicker than other options, and their softness produces more
brake dust
. As such, organic brake pads are often recommended for city drivers who don't frequently use the highway.

[IMG:2]

The word "ceramic" may not be something you think of when it comes to brake pads, but ceramic brake pads are an excellent choice for many drivers. These brake pads are made mostly of dense, durable ceramic, as well as other materials to help with friction and heat distribution. Originally, ceramic brake pads also had copper fibers in them, but after the EPA launched the Copper-Free Brake Initiative in 2015, the fibers have since been removed.

Ceramic brake pads are often on the quiet side — less so than metallic pads but a bit louder than organic ones — but their real strength lies in their durability. Ceramic pads have a longer lifespan than their organic and metallic counterparts, and due to their material, they also produce the least amount of brake dust. But ceramic brake pads are expensive, more so than other brake pad types, so this performance comes at a cost.

[IMG:3]

Also, ceramic brake pads take longer to heat up (though they have great heat dispersion overall) and won't perform well in extremely cold temperatures. That said, ceramic brake pads will be ideal for those who drive further and more often than their city-driving counterparts. If you're on the highway a lot or drive a lot for work, it's a good idea to look into ceramic brake pads for your next replacement.

Metallic and semi-metallic brake pads are on the opposite end of the scale from organic brake pads. While full metallic brakes do exist, for any average consumer, you'll be looking at semi-metallic brake pads for your car. Even when a particular manufacturer states that their brake pads are metallic, they will likely be semi-metallic brake pads. While the two names being used interchangeably can be confusing, metallic brakes are only going to be used on very specialized vehicles.

Semi-metallic brake pads are composed of 30-70% metals (typically a mixture of iron, copper, steel, and other metals), and are typically bonded with graphite instead of resin. There are also low-metallic brake pads, which only have 10-30% of metals with inorganic filler. Whether semi-metallic or low metallic, the inclusion of metal makes these brake pads very durable — more so than other pad choices. These brake pads also have great stopping power, distribute heat well, and work well at a wide range of temperatures. Finally, in terms of price, metallic pads are more expensive than organic pads but still less expensive than their ceramic counterparts.

[IMG:4]

However, semi-metallic brake pads are loud, which you might expect from a metallic pad that will create friction against other metallic components — and that grinding will also provide a fair amount of brake dust. In addition, due to the materials, semi-metallic brake pads wear out your
brake rotor
faster than other options on the market. Generally, semi-metallic brake pads are recommended for performance driving and trucking.

There is no brake pad suitable for every situation, so before deciding on a brake pad, you'll need to consider how you drive and what sort of vehicle you have. In many ways, ceramic brake pads will be the best choice for the average driver. These brake pads are quiet, produce the least dust, and are very durable.

[IMG:5]

However, they're also on the expensive side, and if you're not one to drive your car often, they can be overkill. If you keep most of your driving to the city, organic brake pads will likely be a better option — while they wear out faster, they're cheaper and still work well, so if you're not going on the highway or taking road trips often, these will work great.

Semi-metallic brake pads are mainly for those who do more specialized driving than the average person. So they're best suited for long-haul and performance driving, where the superior braking is worth the trade-off of the noise and wearing down your rotors faster.

queue.title: California Governor Signs California Motor Vehicle Glass Act Into Law
queue.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed legislation establishing new requirements for automotive glass repair and replacement businesses, including rules governing advanced driver-assistance system (ADAS) calibration, insurance claims, consumer disclosures and the assignment of insurance benefits.

- California Enacts S.B. 1069, Speeds Conditional Approval for Emissions Parts


Newsom signed S.B. 988, the California Motor Vehicle Glass Act, on Sept. 27. The legislation was authored by Sen. Tim Grayson, D-Concord.

The new law establishes a series of requirements for businesses primarily engaged in automotive glass replacement, including the repair and installation of vehicle windows and windshields. Several provisions are particularly relevant to collision repair facilities that perform glass replacement or ADAS calibration.

[IMG:1]

ADAS Calibration Disclosures Required

The law addresses the increasingly important connection between windshield replacement and ADAS calibration.

Before providing glass repair or replacement services, a motor vehicle glass repair shop must notify the customer whether the vehicle is equipped with ADAS.

If it is, the shop must also disclose whether calibration or recalibration is necessary following windshield repair or replacement based on the vehicle manufacturer’s recommendations and whether the shop intends to perform the calibration according to the manufacturer’s specifications.

If the shop cannot or does not intend to perform the calibration, it must inform the customer that the vehicle should be taken to a manufacturer’s certified dealership or qualified specialist capable of performing the work.

[IMG:2]

When calibration is performed, the shop must provide written notification stating whether it was successful. If the calibration is unsuccessful, the customer must be advised to take the vehicle to a certified dealership or qualified specialist.

The law also requires the shop to advise the customer not to rely on the ADAS until an unsuccessful calibration has been successfully completed.

New Requirements for Insurance-Paid Glass Work

S.B. 988 establishes additional requirements when glass repairs are expected to be paid through a first-party insurance policy.

[IMG:3]

A shop cannot contract with a customer for insurance-paid glass repair or replacement until the customer has made a first-party claim, the shop has received a claim or referral number and applicable ADAS disclosure requirements have been satisfied.

Shops must also provide customers with a good faith estimate of anticipated fees and costs, followed by an updated estimate before performing the service.

[IMG:4]

Upon completion, the customer must receive an itemized invoice and, upon payment, a receipt, along with information concerning the outcome of any ADAS calibration or recalibration.

The law states that shops cannot charge more than “reasonable and customary” fees and costs for glass repairs or replacement and associated ADAS calibration or recalibration recommended by the vehicle manufacturer.

Assignment of Insurance Benefits Restricted

Another significant provision involves the assignment of insurance benefits.

Under the law, an insured with a motor vehicle insurance policy covering windshield and calibration repair or replacement is prohibited from assigning, delegating or otherwise transferring duties, rights or benefits under the policy to another person before or after a loss.

[IMG:5]

Contracts entered into on or after Jan. 1, 2027, that violate the provision are considered void and unenforceable.

The restriction does not prevent an insured from authorizing or directing an insurer to make payment directly to a service provider.

Incentives for Glass Claims Prohibited

The new law also targets incentives used to generate insurance glass claims.

Glass repair shops and others compensated for soliciting insurance claims are prohibited from offering rebates, gifts, gift cards, cash, coupons, prizes, bonuses, payments or other incentives in exchange for directing or making a glass claim under an auto insurance policy.

The law also prohibits several practices related to glass claims, including submitting false, misleading or incomplete information to insurers or insureds; misrepresenting where work was performed; advising customers to falsify the date of damage; falsely signing insurance-related forms; and misrepresenting repair prices.

[IMG:6]

A glass shop also cannot tell a customer that an insurer has approved a repair without directly verifying the coverage or approval and obtaining written or recorded confirmation.

Similarly, a shop cannot represent that a repair will be completely covered by insurance at no cost to the customer unless coverage has been verified.

[IMG:7]

The law also expressly prohibits damaging a vehicle — or encouraging an insured to damage a vehicle — to increase the scope of a glass repair claim.

Consumer Choice Protected

S.B. 988 establishes protections concerning a consumer’s selection of a glass repair or recalibration facility.

An insured making a first-party glass claim cannot be required to use a particular glass shop or recalibration facility to receive insurance benefits.

The law states that consumers may select independent shops, network or non-network shops, affiliated or nonaffiliated repair facilities, dealerships or other qualified specialists.

[IMG:8]

Insurers, insurance producers, adjusters and those acting on their behalf are prohibited from purposefully misleading, threatening or coercing an insured into using — or not using — a particular glass repair shop or recalibration facility.

The law does not prevent an insurer or its representatives from recommending a glass shop, explaining available insurance coverage or maintaining a network of glass repair shops.

Violations Carry Civil Penalties

Violations of the California Motor Vehicle Glass Act carry civil penalties of up to $500 for a first violation and up to $2,000 for each subsequent violation.

[IMG:9]

Those penalties may be pursued through civil actions brought on behalf of the state by a city attorney, county counsel or the California attorney general.

For collision repair businesses that perform automotive glass replacement or ADAS calibration, the new law creates additional documentation and disclosure obligations while also establishing protections surrounding consumers’ ability to select their preferred repair and recalibration providers.

queue.title: Survey shows gas, diesel vehicles most driven in 2025, hybrid and EV miles driven up
queue.text:
The AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety’s newly released 2025 American Driving Survey shows gas and diesel vehicles continued to account for most driving in 2025 at 89.5% of all trips, down from 91% in 2024.

However, a research brief states that hybrid and electric vehicle use did increase last year, representing 7.4% (up 1% from 2024) and 3.1% of trips (up 0.6% from 2024), respectively.

AAA Foundation says the survey is meant to quantify the U.S. population’s daily driving and compare the results with previous years. A research brief explores trends in driving behavior by vehicle age and vehicle type, including differences across population groups. The survey was conducted between Jan. 1, 2023, and Dec. 31, 2025.

U.S. drivers collectively made 232 billion trips, spent 95 billion hours driving, and traveled 2.76 trillion miles last year.

[IMG:1]

Those results were projected to the national population based on a survey of 5,100 participants whose answers showed they made an average of 2.40 driving trips per day, spent 59.3 minutes driving, and traveled 28.6 miles daily.

“Driving patterns in 2025 remained similar to those observed in previous years, with only observed changes in travel exposure and vehicle characteristics,” the brief states. “Drivers traveled slightly fewer miles and spent slightly less time driving compared with 2024, while newer vehicles and vehicles with hybrid or electric powertrains continued to represent a growing share of trips. EV use remained limited but was associated with longer trips compared with conventional vehicles. Continued monitoring of travel behavior, vehicle characteristics, and demographic differences remains important for understanding changes in mobility patterns and their implications for traffic safety in the United States.”

Researchers found that 95% of U.S. residents ages 16 and older reported driving at least occasionally in 2025, a slight increase from 2024.

[IMG:2]

As in previous years, drivers ages 35–49 reported the most daily trips, driving time, and mileage, while drivers ages 16–19 reported the least, according to the brief.

“Driving prevalence increased across most age groups between 2024 and 2025,” the brief states. “The largest significant increase was observed among 16- to 19-year-olds, rising from 83.1% to 91.4%, and for 25- to 34-year-olds (95.5%). Smaller increases were observed across the remaining age groups, with driving rates exceeding 90% for all age categories.”

“Male drivers reported more trips, driving time, and miles than female drivers. “Drivers in the South reported the highest daily driving time and mileage, while drivers in the West reported the lowest. “Drivers with a bachelor’s degree or higher reported more trips and greater driving time and mileage than other education groups. “The distribution of driving trips by vehicle age continued to shift toward newer vehicles, with vehicles aged 0–4 years accounting for the largest share of trips (39.3%), up from 34% in 2024 and 27% in 2023.”

[IMG:3]

“Male drivers reported more trips, driving time, and miles than female drivers.

“Drivers in the South reported the highest daily driving time and mileage, while drivers in the West reported the lowest.

“Drivers with a bachelor’s degree or higher reported more trips and greater driving time and mileage than other education groups.

“The distribution of driving trips by vehicle age continued to shift toward newer vehicles, with vehicles aged 0–4 years accounting for the largest share of trips (39.3%), up from 34% in 2024 and 27% in 2023.”

[IMG:4]

AAA Foundation says that EV trips had the longest average duration and distance compared with gas/diesel and hybrid vehicles. Gas/diesel vehicles averaged 24.3 minutes and 11.8 miles per trip, while hybrids averaged 25 minutes and 12.4 miles.

EV trips had the longest average duration and distance, averaging 30.1 minutes and 13.8 miles per trip.

Hybrid and EV use was highest among drivers with a bachelor’s degree or higher and among drivers located in the West.

As for road trips, 30.1% of survey respondents reported taking at least one road trip in the previous four weeks, with an average one-way trip length of 234.8 miles. Gas/diesel vehicles remained the predominant vehicle type across all groups, accounting for more than 90% of trips in most categories.

queue.title: Brake Job: 2020-2025 GM T1XX Pickups
queue.text:
Brake pad replacement on a T1XX Silverado or Sierra is tied into more systems than the friction material alone. These trucks use an electric brake pad life monitor, axle-specific wear sensors and an electric parking brake at the rear. The brake master cylinder can also pressurize the hydraulic system during an automated self-test. A routine pad job therefore requires a controlled shutdown, correct sensor handling and the proper reset or calibration before the truck leaves the bay.

Here’s one critical safety step: Disconnect the negative battery cable before caliper service so an automated self-test cannot pressurize the master cylinder when a door is opened or the key transmitter wakes the vehicle.

For rear brake work, place the parking brake in Parking Brake Service Mode before disconnecting the battery. Then raise and support the truck using the approved lift points and remove the wheel. Observe normal brake-dust and brake-fluid precautions, and keep fluid off painted surfaces. If a hose is opened, plug both sides immediately to limit fluid loss and contamination. Use new sealing washers during assembly, bleed the hydraulic system, inspect for leaks and restore the reservoir with GM-approved fluid from a clean, sealed container.

[IMG:1]

How the Brake Pad Life Monitor Works

The Driver Information Center normally displays front and rear pad life as a percentage. Near the calculated end of pad life, the message changes to an estimated distance remaining and repeats at ignition cycles so the driver can schedule service. If the system detects a supply-voltage fault, it can label the value invalid.

The Brake System Control Module has one input for the front axle sensor and one for the rear. It supplies voltage to each sensor; the sensors use vehicle ground. Inside each sensor are breakable wire resistors. The module combines that signal with its wear algorithm to calculate the displayed percentage. It is an estimate, so the technician still needs to inspect both sides of each axle. After pads are replaced, perform the Axle Brake Pad Life Monitor Reset Learn..

Rear Caliper and Electronic Parking Brake

The left-rear caliper carries the rear wear sensor. After entering Parking Brake Service Mode and disconnecting the battery, remove the bleeder-valve cap to free the sensor routing, disconnect the electrical connector and remove the sensor from the pad. Replace the rear pads if the sensor has contacted the rotor. Handle the replacement head carefully, reconnect it, reinstall the bleeder cap and reset the brake pad life monitor after the truck is lowered.

[IMG:2]

For complete rear caliper service, disconnect the parking-brake actuator connector. Remove the two actuator bolts, lift off the actuator and discard the actuator-lever seal. If the hydraulic hose is disconnected, discard both sealing washers and plug the hose. Remove the two guide-pin bolts and the caliper. Support the caliper whenever the hose remains attached; never hang it by the hose.

During assembly, tighten the rear guide-pin bolts to specification, use new hose washers and install a new parking-brake actuator-lever seal. Re-fit the actuator, tighten its bolts to the current VIN-specific specification and reconnect its electrical connector. After reconnecting the battery, bleed and leak-check any opened hydraulic circuit.

[IMG:3]

The final step after lowering the truck is Park Brake Calibration. Service Mode and calibration are separate steps: Service Mode prepares the mechanism for work; calibration restores correct operation after service.

Key Torque and Wear Specifications

Verify wheel, brake-hose fitting and parking-brake actuator fastener values in the current VIN-specific service information; those values were not included in the supplied quick-reference sheet.

Rapid rear pad wear – Bulletin 21-NA-089 , dated Oct. 30, 2024, covers 2019-2025 Silverado and Sierra 1500 configurations identified in the bulletin, generally those without RPO RG1. Dirt, mud or debris can pack into the rear calipers and hold the pads against the rotors. When mud is confirmed as the cause, GM calls for shielded calipers with dirt deflectors. The RG1 shielded caliper became a dealer-installed option for 2021, and the bulletin specifically says it can be installed on 2019-2021 light-duty 1500 pickups not built with the option. Current listed parts are 85140318 left and 85140319 right.

[IMG:4]

Excessive brake dust – Bulletin 18-NA-067 , revised May 6, 2024, describes black dust as a normal result of the high-performance pad material, made more visible by large wheel openings. GM recommends a soft cloth, mild soap and water, followed by a clean-water rinse and soft-towel drying. Strong chemicals, acids, abrasive cleaners and abrasive brushes can damage aluminum or chrome wheels and caliper finishes. Do not direct a power washer at the caliper, because it may remove copper paste from the pads and require the lubricant to be reapplied.

Finish the Job as a System

Before release, verify sensor and hose routing, connector engagement, pad-retaining hardware, fluid level and pedal feel. Reset the correct axle’s pad life monitor, perform Park Brake Calibration when the rear actuator or caliper has been serviced, clear related faults and road-test the truck. On these pickups, the friction work is only complete when the electronic monitoring and parking-brake functions are complete too.

queue.title: What You Should Ask Customers Who Want ‘Aggressive’ Brake Pads
queue.text:
When customers request aggressive brake pads, the term can have several meanings. Some want sharper freeway stops. Others want more confidence on winding roads or greater control while towing. Some simply prefer a firmer and more responsive pedal.

Terms such as “aggressive,” “high performance,” and “racing” often appear in marketing. However, they do not always describe what the customer needs.

Technicians should begin by asking questions rather than recommending a product.

Ask About Current Brake Performance

The first question is: “What do you like or dislike about your current brakes?”

Long stopping distances, a soft pedal or inconsistent braking may not indicate a pad problem. Hydraulic faults, caliper issues or master cylinder problems can create similar symptoms.

[IMG:1]

Customers may incorrectly attribute those symptoms to the brake pads.

Technicians should also ask when the brakes were last serviced. A customer who cannot remember may not need a high-performance pad immediately.

In many cases, a premium replacement pad can restore like-new braking feel. This option may meet the customer’s needs without moving to a more aggressive product.

[IMG:2]

Define Expectations for Aggressive Brake Pads

The next question is: “What do you expect an aggressive brake pad to do?”

Advertising, online forums and articles may shape customer expectations before the visit. The technician’s role is to guide those expectations toward the correct application.

After identifying the customer’s preferences, ask how the vehicle operates each day. Determine whether it sees mostly highway driving, winding roads or stop-and-go traffic.

[IMG:3]

Also ask whether the customer regularly tows or hauls. These answers show how often the brakes experience heavy use.

They also indicate whether the brakes usually operate cold or at higher temperatures.

Discuss Noise, Dust and Pad Life

Technicians should explain potential differences in brake noise, dust, pedal feel and pad life. This discussion can prevent misunderstandings and avoidable comebacks.

A brake pad recommendation should follow the complete conversation. Some customers may already prefer a specific brand.

Others may rely on the technician’s recommendation. In either case, product research helps separate verified performance characteristics from marketing claims.

queue.title: Understanding Brake Pad Wear Sensors for Imports
queue.text:
At one time, brake pad wear sensors were a pretty simple matter: the sensor was just a spring steel tab that was mounted on the backing plate and bent at a right angle. The tab was as long as the minimum depth for the pad’s friction material, so when the pad wore down to that minimum depth the tab would drag on the brake rotor and cause an unmistakable metal-on-metal screech that would alert the driver that it was time for new brakes. Unfortunately, many drivers don’t even know what that screech means or may not notice it in a vehicle that’s got a lot of sound deadening, and by the time they bring their car into the shop the rotors are already chewed up (and the vehicle is very unsafe to drive).

While many brake pads, both OEM and aftermarket, still feature these simple wear indicators, newer systems are more sophisticated. That means giving a driver a heads-up long before the pads get down to minimum thickness and start damaging the rotors through metal-to-metal contact.

Brake Wear Sensor Designs

Older brake pad wear sensors consisted of a loop of wire embedded in the friction material at a certain depth, with a low amount of current running through it  and the sensor looped into the vehicle’s ABS circuit and processor. This sensor had a known resistance value; when resistance would be above 2000 ohms, a rectifier circuit would read that as an open circuit and would light up an indicator on the dash. These designs could be prone to corrosion or physical damage (sometimes just due to heat from the brakes), and it was always recommended that the sensor be replaced along with the pads when it was time for a brake job.

[IMG:1]

Newer sensor designs are capable of actually giving a driver an estimate of the number of miles that are left on the pads. The key difference is that they’re designed with two resistor circuits in parallel with each other. The first circuit is set at a higher position in the sensor, with the second in a lower position. When the first circuit is broken, the parallel design means that the resistance will increase. If the second wire is broken, the circuit is then read as open, triggering the warning light on the dash.

With these two-stage sensor systems, the first circuit usually won’t trigger a warning light. Instead, the system starts to calculate remaining pad life with information about wheel rotational speed, mileage, brake pressure, brake rotor and pad temperature and total brake operating time. Splicing wires together to bypass the sensor won’t work – the module confirms the sensor is working by  passing voltage through the circuit. Splicing wires together would mean the system would read it as an open circuit and would set the dash warning light.

Most vehicles will have one sensor for the front axle and one for the rear, although some might be equipped with a sensor for each wheel. Some systems are designed for two-stage warnings, sometimes with a yellow indicator light for the first stage and a red light for when brake pad replacement is imminent.

[IMG:2]

Considering that the wire loop is destroyed as part of normal wear, it’s necessary to replace the sensor when doing a brake job. Even if the customer gets the vehicle in early and the sensors haven’t been triggered, the old sensors will already be partially worn and could have damaged leads. Be sure you’re using the proper sensors for the vehicle’s year/make/model, as different sensors have different lead lengths, connector types and mounting designs.

For Mercedes-Benz, Audi, Volkswagen, Mini and BMW models, it’s necessary to perform a reset after replacing the pads and sensors.

[IMG:3]

While the process can vary from one year/make/model to another, a typical reset might involve these steps:

Turn on the ignition by pressing the start/stop button once or twice without your foot on the brake pedal (don’t start the engine).

Wait for all the dashboard lights and chimes to finish.

Find the BC button on the turn signal stalk to cycle through until it displays time and mileage/trip odometer.

Press and hold the odometer reset button until you see a service menu on the instrument cluster.

Use the stalk button to scroll through the options until you see the Brake Pad Service icon.

Press and hold the button again until “Reset?” appears.

Release the button quickly, then press and hold again until the reset occurs and the mileage counter is updated.

For BMW models, this may have to be done through the vehicle’s iDrive system.

Installing the Replacement Sensors

Installation is usually a pretty simple affair. Locate the wire that runs from the brake pad to the wheel well housing or junction box, and undo any fender liner clips or protective access doors. Unplug the sensor by pushing the plastic release tab on its connector. If there are any guide clips along the brake line, carefully unclip them. The sensor can then be pulled or pried from its slot on the interior brake pad. Installation is the reverse of removal, as you push the new sensor head firmly into the slot on the pad and route the wire along the exact same path as before. Be sure to reinstall any clips, rubber grommets or brackets.

queue.title: 2004-2013 Mazda 3 Brake Job
queue.text:
Despite its age, the 2004-2013 Mazda 3 is a popular car you may very well see come through the shop —especially those on the tail end of that year range. Let’s go over the step-by-step brake job process.

The 2004-2013 Mazda 3 is based on the Ford global C1 platform, shared with the European Ford Focus and Volvo S40. Nothing is really groundbreaking about the mechanical brake system, but not paying attention to the details can end in a post-brake-job comeback.

A key service issue concerns the hydraulics and ABS system. The older the car, the greater the chance the brake fluid has not been serviced. Over time this can cause issues with the ABS hydraulic control unit.

[IMG:1]

For almost 10 years, Mazda used the same caliper, pad and rotor design. Pads should be replaced when there is 2mm or less of friction material. If the rotors are any thicker, they have enough material on them to last at least one turning on the lathe. The runout specification for these vehicles is .002” and disc thickness variation should be far below .0005”.

Mazda claims repeated panic braking may raise the temperature in some portions of the disc plate by approx. 1,000°C (l,832°F). This temperature is almost near impossible to achieve this side of a high-speed police chase.

The calipers mount to the brackets using caliper guide pins with Allen heads. The sleeves and boots should be disassembled, cleaned and lubricated every time the brakes are replaced. The torque for the guide pins is 21 ft./lbs. and the caliper bracket bolts should be tightened to 75 ft./lbs.

[IMG:2]

All Mazda3 models have rear disc brakes. The calipers mount to the brackets using caliper guide pins with Allen heads. The sleeves and boots should be disassembled, cleaned and lubricated every time the brakes are replaced. The torque for the guide pins is 21 ft./lbs. and the caliper bracket bolts should be tightened to 55 ft./lbs.

Mazda uses a hand brake that is incorporated into the rear caliper, and a couple of systems are employed to retract rear pistons. The later-model cars require the familiar method of turning the piston clockwise while applying pressure, where others will have a plug on the back side of the caliper that provides access for an Allen wrench to facilitate retracting the piston. Be careful as you retract the piston.

[IMG:3]

After the pads are replaced, pump the pedal and adjust the parking brake mechanism in the rear calipers. If the level has too much travel, perform the following steps:

Pump the brake pedal a few times.

Remove the service hole cover of the rear console.

Turn the adjusting nut and adjust the parking brake lever.

After adjustment, pull the parking brake lever one notch and verify that the parking brake warning light illuminates and the rear brakes do not drag.

ABS/DSC Diagnostics and Repair

The Mazda3 comes in two styles, ABS and ABS with Dynamic Stability Control (DSC). Both systems connect to other vehicle components via a high-speed serial data bus. The DSC system ties more components together (like a yaw/pitch sensor and steering position sensor) onto the bus.

[IMG:4]

If you are seeing communication-related DTCs, it is essential that you fully diagnose problems with the system before you start replacing sensors and modules. Some of these vehicles have been on the road for more than six years and the connections will be starting to corrode and fret.

One of the main facilitators of ABS/DCS problems are the connectors, especially under the hood where the control/modulator unit connects. Being able to measure values at the connectors and observe data on a scan tool is essential for diagnosing problems.

The biggest ABS issue with the three generations of Mazda 3 is power. With some higher mileage vehicles, the battery cables, wiring from the power distribution box or the ground connection (behind the driver’s side headlight at G02) can have enough resistance so the voltage drops below 8 volts. When this happens, the ABS module cuts control and the electronic brake distribution system is disabled.

[IMG:5]

If a modulator/control unit is replaced, the pressure sensors must be recalibrated with a scan tool that is able to communicate with the chassis/ABS module. If this is not performed, it can result in brake failure and lock up.

If you have DTCs C1141, C1142, C1143, C1144, C1233, C1234, C1235 or C1236 (ABS wheel-speed sensor/ABS sensor rotor), chances are something is wrong with the wheel bearings. Another cause for these codes could be an accumulation of metal debris on the sensor. The front bearings are press-in cartridge-style units. Rear wheel bearings are hub units. In the front, the tone ring, or encoder, is on the inner seal of the bearing and the sensor is mounted in the knuckle. The parameters for these codes to be set include abnormalities in the signal such as a weak signal or large differences in the value when compared to the other sensors.

[IMG:6]

If you have DTCs C1145, C1155, C1165 or C1175 (open sensor), it could be damaged wiring or a failed sensor that is the problem. If you have more than one, chances are there is a problem with the connection at the control unit or in the front or rear harnesses of the sensors.

These DTCs will usually clear themselves after repairs are made and the vehicle is driven above 6.2 mph when the self-diagnostic check is performed.

Some customers may report a slight clunk, bang or jolt from the front of the vehicle. This concern will most likely occur during the vehicle’s first forward movement and after the vehicle sits for a few hours and/or a cold soak. This is a normal operating noise of the ABS system.

[IMG:7]

If you encounter a customer complaint for this concern, explain that the noise comes from the ABS/TCS/DSC “Malfunction Detection Function” initial check. The initial check is a necessary function to ensure the normal operation of the ABS/TCS/DSC system. This initial test function occurs during the vehicle’s first forward movement and when the vehicle reaches approximately 6.2 mph.

This article was originally published by our sister publication, Brake & Front End, in 2019 . It is being reissued here as part of our “From the Archives” series.

queue.title: Euro 7-Compliant Vehicles Will Change Brake and Tire Service
queue.text:
If you specialize in European vehicles, you already know that some are engineered differently from their domestic counterparts because of European emissions and safety regulations. It has been this way for more than 60 years.

Most of those differences have involved components under the hood or in the exhaust system. Euro 7 changes that pattern by placing brake and tire wear under regulatory scrutiny.

These requirements will not change how you service vehicles next week. However, they have the potential to influence brake-system designs, friction materials, rotor construction, replacement tires and the types of vehicles entering your shop over the next decade.

[IMG:1]

Previous European emissions standards created service opportunities involving oxygen sensors, diesel particulate filters, selective catalytic reduction systems and other components. Euro 7’s brake and tire provisions could have the opposite effect by extending some replacement intervals. At the same time, they could make selecting and installing the correct replacement components more important—and potentially more expensive.

Internal-combustion engines now operate at historically low levels of particulate matter and other regulated pollutants. Battery-electric vehicles produce no tailpipe emissions, but they still generate particles from their brakes and tires. As exhaust emissions decline, these non-exhaust sources represent a larger portion of the particles attributed to road transportation.

European Union Regulation 2024/1257, commonly known as Euro 7, introduces limits on brake-particle emissions from passenger cars and light commercial vehicles for the first time.

[IMG:2]

Beginning November 29, 2026, newly approved passenger-car and light-commercial-vehicle types must comply with Euro 7.

The initial brake-emission limit for most passenger vehicles is 7 milligrams per kilometer. The limit for battery-electric passenger vehicles is 3 milligrams per kilometer. These limits apply to PM10—the mass of airborne particles with an aerodynamic diameter of 10 microns or smaller.

Brake emissions are measured according to procedures based on United Nations Global Technical Regulation No. 24. A complete brake corner is operated on an inertia dynamometer inside a controlled enclosure. The brake is subjected to a standardized cycle intended to represent urban, rural and highway operation. Instruments collect and measure the particles released during the test.

The regulation distinguishes among powertrain configurations and accounts for the amount of braking performed by the friction brakes. That gives electrified vehicles an advantage because regenerative braking converts vehicle motion into electrical energy rather than heat and wear at the pads and rotors.

[IMG:3]

The important distinction is that Euro 7 measures airborne wear material. It is not a stopping-distance, pedal-feel or friction-equivalency standard. A replacement pad might comply with a traditional performance requirement such as UN Regulation No. 90 and still require separate evaluation for brake-particle emissions.

Producing friction between a brake pad and rotor inevitably removes some material. The amount released depends on the friction formulation, rotor metallurgy, surface treatment, temperature, pressure and how the two components interact.

[IMG:4]

A pad with a low wear rate does not automatically produce low emissions. Material removed from the pad or rotor can remain attached to the components, fall to the road as larger debris or become suspended in the air as fine particles. Consequently, manufacturers must evaluate the pad and rotor as a system.

European manufacturers and brake suppliers are pursuing several solutions. One is the development of new friction formulations designed to reduce wear without sacrificing stopping performance, temperature stability, noise control or pedal feel.

Another solution is a more wear-resistant rotor surface. Manufacturers are experimenting with hard-metal coatings, laser-applied coatings and other surface treatments that can reduce both rotor wear and corrosion. Some vehicles already use coated rotors, particularly on electrified applications where regenerative braking can leave the friction brakes unused for extended periods.

[IMG:5]

Installing a low-cost pad against an expensive coated rotor—or replacing a coated rotor with a conventional casting—could alter noise, wear, pedal feel and particle emissions. Matching the pad and rotor may become more important than selecting either component separately.

Longer pad and rotor life could reduce the frequency of conventional brake jobs. However, that does not mean electrified vehicles will be maintenance-free. Reduced friction-brake use can promote rotor corrosion, uneven contact patterns, sticking pads and seized caliper hardware. Shops may perform fewer wear-related brake jobs but more services involving corrosion, electronic parking brakes, brake-by-wire systems and preventive cleaning and lubrication.

Euro 7 also establishes a framework for limiting tire abrasion, but its implementation follows a different schedule. Requirements for new C1 passenger-car tire types are scheduled to begin July 1, 2028, and expand to all new C1 tires placed on the European market beginning July 1, 2030.

[IMG:6]

Unlike brake testing, tire-abrasion testing can use standardized road-convoy or laboratory-drum procedures. Tire mass loss is measured over a prescribed distance and under controlled conditions. Tread-depth measurements and scanning can support the evaluation, but the objective is to determine how much material the tire loses—not merely how quickly the visible tread disappears.

Developing a low-abrasion tire involves compromises among tread life, wet braking, dry grip, rolling resistance, noise and ride quality. A hard compound may wear slowly but cannot be allowed to compromise wet traction. A soft, high-performance tire may produce excellent grip but wear quickly and release more material.

[IMG:7]

Electrified vehicles do not have an automatic advantage in tire testing. Regenerative braking reduces friction-brake use, but the additional mass of a traction battery and the immediate torque produced by an electric motor can increase tire wear. Alignment, inflation pressure, suspension condition, driving style and rotation practices will remain critical.

Technicians should pay close attention to load index, speed rating and vehicle-specific tire approvals. BMW’s star marking, Mercedes-Benz’s MO designation and Audi’s AO marking, for example, identify tires developed for specific vehicle requirements. A tire that fits physically may not provide the intended rolling resistance, noise characteristics, range, handling or wear performance.

Not every European-brand vehicle sold in the United States is imported from Europe. Based on 2025 sales, approximately 36% of the BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen, Audi and MINI vehicles sold here were assembled in the United States. About 39% came from Europe, while the remaining 26% were primarily manufactured in Mexico or other countries.

[IMG:8]

However, manufacturers increasingly develop vehicles as global platforms. A brake system or tire package engineered to satisfy Euro 7 may also appear on a U.S.-market vehicle even when that vehicle is assembled in South Carolina, Alabama, Tennessee or Mexico. Maintaining separate brake hardware and friction formulations for different markets can be more expensive than using a common design.

This means U.S. shops could begin encountering Euro 7-influenced brake systems before any comparable American brake-emission regulation takes effect.

The other important development is the growth of plug-in hybrid technology. PHEVs can reduce friction-brake use through regenerative braking without depending entirely on charging infrastructure. BMW sold 25,351 PHEVs in the United States during 2025, an increase of 30.7% over 2024. Mercedes-Benz has also expanded its PHEV lineup with vehicles such as the GLE 450e and GLC 350e.

[IMG:9]

The maintenance cost of these vehicles remains to be seen. Brake components may last longer, but coated rotors, application-specific pads, electronic controls and approved replacement tires could increase the cost of each service. Keeping these vehicles operating as designed may require more precise parts selection and closer adherence to service information than on previous models.

We are just at the start of Euro 7 emissions-compliant vehicles, but now is the time to look at a strategy for your shop in the future. The first strategy is to keep abreast of the latest replacement European brake components that meet or exceed OE specifications. That is where the Import Car website and newsletter can help. Also, it is clear from the growing sales of hybrid vehicles and the increasing number of models that training on how to service these vehicles needs to become a priority over the next five years.

queue.title: The Whens and Whys of Intermittent Belt Noise
queue.text:
Imagine being a belt on the front of the engine. Yours is a balancing act that is always being upset by change from the inputs from the crank pulley and the loads from the alternator, AC compressor and maybe a power steering pump. Your mission is to keep in contact with the grooves on the pulleys. You can’t hold on too tightly, because it could decrease fuel economy and damage the bearings inside the water pump, idler bushings and other components. But you can’t be too loose because it will cause you to slip, resulting in wear and noise.
